L25: TL;DR
L26: The binary asks for three positive integers a, b, c, checks a > b > c > 0, evaluates a large statically linked MPC/MPFR-style expression at 10000-bit precision, and reads flag.txt only if the check passes.
L27: 
L28: A valid input is:
L29: ```
L30: 20260869859883222379931520298326390700152988332214525711323500132179943287700005601210288797153868533207131302477269470450828233936557
L31: 19042526617180316524139256060457587477079898033904404413796747301621619442196095529358289579194164508926431543186710461288793130962534

L19: ## krwd
L20: 
L21: by 【16†rawpayload】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Tags: kernel
L24: 
L25: Rating:
L26: This challenge is a Linux kernel pwnable built around a custom character device, /dev/chall. The bug is a classic delayed user-pointer bug: the module stores a __user pointer in a global request and later dereferences it from a kernel workqueue thread. Because the copy runs in a kworker instead of the process that submitted the ioctl, the user address is interpreted in whichever userspace address space the kworker is borrowing at that moment.
L27: On this VM, QEMU is single CPU (-smp 1). By repeatedly waking PID 1 (/init, BusyBox ash) and scheduling delayed work, the kworker can be made to perform copy_from_user() and copy_to_user() against PID 1's active_mm. That gives a probabilistic arbitrary read/write primitive into PID 1 userspace.
L28:

L25: Flag 1 is reachable through the patched d8 binary by abusing the Maglev heap-object-check omission. The exploit mutates one V8 string object while the native triforce() callback is sleeping between its three string comparisons.

L19: ## wandering
L20: 
L21: by 【16†hattorihanzo1111】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: 
L25: 1. Recon
L26: 
L27: $ ls
L28: compose.yaml Dockerfile flag.txt 【18†run.sh†run.sh】 vm
L29: $ file vm
L30: ELF 64-bit LSB pie executable, x86-64, dynamically linked, stripped
L31: The Dockerfile wires a socat -T 60 TCP-LISTEN:1337,reuseaddr,fork EXEC:/app/【18†run.sh†run.sh】 to a shell that loops the VM forever:
L32: 
L33: while true; do "$VM_BIN" || true; done
L34: So a single TCP connection can run many VM instances back-to-back — each starts fresh, with a new seed.
L35: Useful strings recovered from the binary:
L36: 
L37: %d%c%d
L38: /flag.txt
L39: incorrect!
L40: correct!
L41: Failed initialization
L42: %d%c%d immediately tells us input is <int><char><int> per record.
L43: 
L44: The repeating pattern 22 49 40 22 ... in .data (visible as "I@" in the hex dump) is suspicious — it hints at a fixed bytecode table where many instructions share a leading dword.
L45:
